# Pre-training and Scaling Large Language Models {#pre-training-and-scaling-large-language-models}

After scoping a use case, the next lifecycle decision (Section
\@ref(generative-ai-project-lifecycle)) is which model to build on. Almost
always the answer is an existing pre-trained model. This chapter explains why,
covering:

- how pre-training works;
- why training large models strains GPU memory, and the techniques that make
  it feasible (number formats and distributed training);
- the scaling laws that link model size, data, and compute; and
- the narrow case where pre-training your own domain model can be worth it.

## Choosing a starting model

Open models are distributed through **model hubs** such as Hugging Face. Each
model ships with a **model card** [@mitchell2019modelcards]. The card records
the intended uses, training data and procedure, evaluation results, and known
limitations. Read it before anything else. It tells you whether the model's
architecture, licence, languages, and context length fit your task.

## Pre-training objectives and architecture families

**Pre-training** is self-supervised learning on a very large text corpus. The
labels come from the text itself, so no human annotation is needed. What the
model learns to do depends on its training objective, and the objective is
tied to its architecture:

| Family | Pre-training objective | What the model sees | Good at | Examples |
|:-------|:-----------------------|:--------------------|:--------|:---------|
| **Encoder-only** (autoencoding) | **Masked language modelling**: predict randomly masked tokens | Both sides of each token (bidirectional) | Classification, named-entity recognition, embeddings | BERT [@devlin2019bert], RoBERTa [@liu2019roberta] |
| **Decoder-only** (autoregressive) | **Causal language modelling**: predict the next token | Only earlier tokens (left-to-right) | Text generation; at scale, zero-shot and few-shot on many tasks | GPT [@brown2020gpt3], BLOOM, Llama |
| **Encoder–decoder** (sequence-to-sequence) | Varies. T5 uses **span corruption**: masked spans are replaced by sentinel tokens, and the decoder reconstructs them | Encoder: whole input; decoder: earlier outputs | Translation, summarization, input-to-output tasks | T5 [@raffel2020t5], BART |

The two main losses, for a token sequence $x_1, \dots, x_T$:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{causal}} = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}),
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\text{masked}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\setminus \mathcal{M}})
$$

Here $\mathcal{M}$ is the set of masked positions. BERT masks about 15% of
tokens [@devlin2019bert].

Today's general-purpose LLMs are almost all decoder-only. Encoder models
remain the workhorses for classification and embeddings.

**Data.** Pre-training corpora contain trillions of tokens drawn from web
crawls, books, code, and curated collections. Raw web text needs heavy
processing: language identification, quality filtering, deduplication, removal
of personal data, and toxicity filtering. This usually discards a large share
of the raw crawl. If you ever plan to pre-train, budget data collection for
that loss. Filtering reduces some risks but does not guarantee unbiased or
safe data.

## Why training does not fit on one GPU {#memory-challenges-in-training-llms}

Storing a model is cheap compared with training it. At 32-bit precision each
parameter takes 4 bytes, so 1 billion parameters need **4 GB** just for the
weights. Training also needs, for every parameter:

| Component | FP32 training (bytes/param) | Mixed-precision training (bytes/param) |
|:----------|---------------------------:|---------------------------------------:|
| Weights used in forward/backward | 4 | 2 (16-bit copy) |
| Gradients | 4 | 2 |
| Adam optimizer: momentum + variance | 8 | 8 (kept in FP32) |
| FP32 master copy of weights | — | 4 |
| **Total, before activations** | **16** | **16** |

**Activations** come on top. These are the intermediate outputs saved for the
backward pass, and they grow with batch size and sequence length.
**Activation checkpointing** saves memory by storing only some activations and
recomputing the rest during the backward pass [@chen2016checkpointing].

Rules of thumb:

- **Training needs roughly 4–6× the memory of the FP32 weights.** That is
  about 16 GB for a 1B-parameter model before activations, and around 24 GB
  with a typical allowance for activations.
- **A 175B-parameter model needs about 2.8 TB** for weights, gradients, and
  optimizer states alone. No single GPU comes close.
- **Fine-tuning has the same profile** when all weights are updated. That is
  the main motivation for PEFT (Section \@ref(peft)).

Two levers reduce the problem: smaller number formats (next section) and
splitting the work across GPUs (the section after).

## Number formats and quantization {#quantization-techniques}

A floating-point number has three parts: a sign bit, **exponent** bits that set
the **range**, and **fraction** (mantissa) bits that set the **precision**.

| Format | Sign / exponent / fraction bits | Bytes | Largest value | $\pi$ stored as |
|:-------|:-------------------------------|------:|:--------------|:----------------|
| FP32 | 1 / 8 / 23 | 4 | $\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ | 3.1415927 |
| FP16 | 1 / 5 / 10 | 2 | 65,504 | 3.140625 |
| BF16 | 1 / 8 / 7 | 2 | $\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ | 3.140625 |
| INT8 | 8-bit integer, $-128$ to $127$ | 1 | Set by a scale factor | Depends on the scale (see below) |

**FP16 vs. BF16.** Both use 2 bytes and, for $\pi$, give the same rounded
value. The difference is range. FP16 overflows above 65,504, so FP16 training
needs *loss scaling* to keep small gradients from underflowing to zero
[@micikevicius2018mixed]. **BF16** (brain floating point, from Google Brain)
keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits. It trades precision for the full FP32 range,
which makes training more stable. That is why it became the default 16-bit
training format on hardware that supports it.

**Mixed-precision training** runs the forward and backward passes in 16-bit
but keeps an FP32 master copy of the weights for the optimizer update
[@micikevicius2018mixed]. This gives most of the speed and activation-memory
benefit of 16-bit arithmetic while preserving update accuracy.

**Integer quantization** maps real values to integers through a scale factor
$s$. With symmetric quantization, $q = \text{round}(x / s)$ and
$s = \max|x| / 127$. Precision therefore depends on the range of the values
being quantized. For example, if the largest weight magnitude in a tensor is
4.0, then $s = 4/127 \approx 0.0315$. $\pi$ is stored as $q = 100$ and
recovered as $100 \times 0.0315 \approx 3.150$. Choosing $s$ well is the
central problem. **Quantization-aware training** learns the scale factors
during training. **Post-training quantization** estimates them afterwards
(Section \@ref(post-training-quantization)).

> **Current practice (October 2026).** BF16 mixed precision is the baseline
> for training. Recent accelerators also support 8-bit floating-point (FP8)
> formats. Large models have been trained with FP8 mixed precision, for example
> DeepSeek-V3 [@deepseek2024v3]. For inference, 8-bit and 4-bit weight
> quantization are routine.

## Distributed training

Multiple GPUs serve two purposes: **speed** (process more data in parallel)
and **capacity** (fit a model that one GPU cannot hold).

### Data parallelism (DDP)

**Distributed data parallel** (PyTorch DDP) puts a full copy of the model on
every GPU and gives each GPU a different slice of every batch. After the
backward pass, gradients are averaged across GPUs (an *all-reduce*), so every
copy applies the same update and stays identical. DDP speeds up training
almost linearly, but **each GPU must hold the full model, its gradients, and
its optimizer states**. It adds speed, not capacity.

### Sharding: ZeRO and FSDP

Under DDP, every GPU stores identical copies of the same states, which is pure
redundancy. **ZeRO** (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) [@rajbhandari2020zero]
**shards** these states across the $N_d$ data-parallel GPUs instead, in three
progressive stages. With $\Psi$ parameters and mixed-precision Adam (2 + 2 + 12
bytes per parameter), the memory per GPU is:

| Stage | What is sharded | Memory per GPU | 7.5B params, 64 GPUs |
|:------|:----------------|:---------------|---------------------:|
| Baseline (DDP) | Nothing | $16\Psi$ | 120 GB |
| ZeRO-1 | Optimizer states | $4\Psi + 12\Psi / N_d$ | 31.4 GB |
| ZeRO-2 | + gradients | $2\Psi + 14\Psi / N_d$ | 16.6 GB |
| ZeRO-3 | + parameters | $16\Psi / N_d$ | 1.9 GB |

Stages 1 and 2 cut memory by up to about 4× and 8×. Stage 3 cuts it in
proportion to the number of GPUs. The example column is the paper's own
illustration.

**Fully Sharded Data Parallel** (PyTorch FSDP) [@zhao2023fsdp] implements the
same idea natively in PyTorch:

1. Before computing a layer, each GPU **gathers** that layer's full parameters
   from the other GPUs (*all-gather*).
2. It runs the forward or backward computation, then **frees** the gathered
   copy.
3. After the backward pass, gradients are **reduced and re-sharded**
   (*reduce-scatter*), so each GPU updates only its own shard.

The cost is extra communication. FSDP exposes this trade-off as a **sharding
strategy**:

- *Full sharding*: most memory saved, most communication.
- *No sharding*: equivalent to DDP.
- *Hybrid sharding*: shard within a machine and replicate across machines,
  keeping heavy traffic on fast local links.
- *CPU offload*: parameters or optimizer states can be moved to CPU memory, at
  a further speed cost.

### Model parallelism

Sharding still runs each layer whole on one GPU at a time. The largest models
also split the computation itself:

- **Tensor parallelism** splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. This
  is the Megatron-LM approach [@shoeybi2019megatron]. It needs very fast
  interconnects, so it is usually kept within one machine.
- **Pipeline parallelism** places different layers on different GPUs and
  streams micro-batches through them to keep all stages busy
  [@huang2019gpipe].

Frontier training combines data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism ("3D
parallelism") with sharding. As GPU count grows, communication overhead lowers
the throughput per GPU. That is a real cost when planning a training run.

## Scaling laws {#scaling-laws}

Pre-training minimizes next-token loss. Three quantities determine how low the
loss goes: model size $N$ (parameters), dataset size $D$ (training tokens),
and compute $C$. For dense transformers, training compute is approximately

$$
C \approx 6ND \quad \text{FLOPs.}
$$

Large budgets are often quoted in **petaFLOP/s-days**. One petaFLOP/s-day is
$10^{15}$ operations per second sustained for a day, which is
$8.64 \times 10^{19}$ FLOPs. GPT-3 175B, trained on 300B tokens, used about
$3.14 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs, or roughly **3,640 petaFLOP/s-days**
[@brown2020gpt3]. That matches $6 \times 175\text{B} \times 300\text{B}$.

### Kaplan et al.: loss follows power laws

@kaplan2020scaling found that test loss falls as a **power law** in each of
$N$, $D$, and $C$, provided the other two are not the bottleneck. For example,
$L(N) \approx (N_c / N)^{\alpha_N}$ with $\alpha_N \approx 0.076$. On log–log
axes these are straight lines over many orders of magnitude. That makes loss
**predictable**: small, cheap runs forecast the loss of large ones.

In practice compute is the hard constraint (hardware, time, money). The
practical question is therefore: **for a fixed compute budget, how should it
be split between a bigger model and more data?** Kaplan et al. recommended
putting most extra compute into model size. That reasoning shaped the very
large models of 2020–21.

### Chinchilla: scale data and parameters together

@hoffmann2022chinchilla revisited the question with more careful experiments,
including learning-rate schedules matched to each run's length. They fitted
the loss as

$$
L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}.
$$

Here $E$ is the irreducible loss of the data, and the two other terms are the
penalties for finite model size and finite data. Minimizing this subject to
$C \approx 6ND$ gives the main result: **$N$ and $D$ should grow in roughly
equal proportion**, which works out to about **20 training tokens per
parameter**. This is a historical empirical estimate for their model family
and setup, not a universal constant.

The test: **Chinchilla** (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) used the same compute
as Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens). It outperformed Gopher, GPT-3, and
other much larger models on a wide range of downstream tasks. Measured against
the 20× rule, many earlier models were *over-parameterized and under-trained*:

| Model | Parameters | Chinchilla-optimal tokens (~20×) | Actual training tokens |
|:------|-----------:|---------------------------------:|-----------------------:|
| GPT-3 [@brown2020gpt3] | 175B | ~3.5T | 300B |
| BLOOM | 176B | ~3.5T | ~366B |
| Chinchilla [@hoffmann2022chinchilla] | 70B | ~1.4T | 1.4T |
| LLaMA-65B | 65B | ~1.3T | 1.4T |

**Interpreting scaling laws:**

- They predict **pre-training loss**, not specific downstream abilities.
  Individual skills can improve unevenly.
- They hold for the architecture, data mixture, and recipe they were fitted
  on. Change those and you must re-fit.
- "Compute-optimal" optimizes **training** compute only. It ignores the cost
  of serving the model afterwards.

> **Current practice (October 2026).** The last point changed practice. A
> model that will serve billions of requests is cheaper overall if it is
> smaller and trained on *far more* than 20 tokens per parameter
> [@sardana2024beyond]. Llama 3's 8B model, for example, was trained on about
> 15T tokens, close to 1,900 tokens per parameter [@dubey2024llama3].
> "Over-training" small models is now normal. Chinchilla remains the reference
> point for the training-compute trade-off.

## Domain adaptation and pre-training your own model

You rarely need to pre-train. The exception is a domain whose **language** is
poorly represented in general corpora:

- **Rare terms**: legal terms such as *mens rea* and *res judicata*.
- **Everyday words with special meanings**: *consideration* in contract law
  means the value exchanged that makes an agreement binding, not kindness.
- **Shorthand**: a prescription note like "1 tab po qid pc & hs" means one
  tablet by mouth four times a day, after meals and at bedtime.

A model learns its vocabulary and representations in pre-training. Later
stages build on those, so a domain the model barely saw may be handled
poorly. Before committing to from-scratch training, climb this ladder of
options, from cheapest to most expensive:

1. Prompting and retrieval (Chapter \@ref(llm-applications)).
2. Fine-tuning or PEFT on domain tasks (Chapter
   \@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation)).
3. **Continued (domain-adaptive) pre-training.** Keep pre-training an existing
   model on unlabelled domain text. @gururangan2020dapt showed consistent
   downstream gains from this across biomedical, computer-science, news, and
   review domains.
4. **Pre-training from scratch** on a mixed domain and general corpus.

### Case study: BloombergGPT

BloombergGPT [@wu2023bloomberggpt] is the best-known from-scratch domain
model:

- **Model and data.** A 50.6B-parameter decoder trained on a corpus of about
  51% financial text (Bloomberg's own and public financial data) and 49%
  general public text. The general data preserved broad language ability.
- **Compute.** About 1.3 million A100 GPU-hours.
- **Scaling choices.** The authors used Chinchilla scaling laws to size the
  model for their budget, and the parameter count landed close to
  compute-optimal. The training tokens (569B) fell *short* of the
  compute-optimal amount, because there was not enough high-quality financial
  text. Real data limits forced a trade-off.
- **Result.** The paper reports that BloombergGPT outperformed similarly sized
  open models on financial tasks by clear margins while staying competitive on
  general-purpose benchmarks.

The lesson is that from-scratch domain pre-training is justified only when the
domain language is distinctive, high-quality domain data exists at scale, and
the compute budget is large.

> **Current practice (October 2026).** Given how capable general models now
> are, combined with continued pre-training, fine-tuning, and retrieval,
> from-scratch domain pre-training is a rare choice. Justify it with an
> evaluation showing that the cheaper options fall short.

## Key takeaways

- Encoder-only models (masked LM) suit understanding tasks; decoder-only
  models (causal LM) suit generation; encoder–decoder models suit
  input-to-output tasks. Start from an existing model and read its model card.
- Training memory is about 16 bytes per parameter before activations, which
  is about 4× the FP32 weights. Large models therefore cannot train on one GPU.
- BF16 keeps FP32's range at half the memory. Mixed precision keeps an FP32
  master copy for stable updates. Integer quantization depends on a scale
  factor.
- DDP replicates the model for speed. ZeRO/FSDP shard optimizer states,
  gradients, and parameters for capacity, at a communication cost. Tensor and
  pipeline parallelism split the computation itself.
- Loss scales as a power law in parameters, data, and compute. Chinchilla
  showed that compute-optimal training scales $N$ and $D$ together (~20
  tokens/parameter). Inference costs now push towards smaller, over-trained
  models.
- Domain pre-training (BloombergGPT) is the expensive end of a ladder that
  starts with prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and continued pre-training.

## Interview checkpoints

- **Masked vs. causal language modelling?** Masked LM predicts hidden tokens
  using both sides of the context. Causal LM predicts the next token using
  only earlier ones.
- **How much GPU memory does training a 7B-parameter model need?** With mixed
  precision and Adam, about 16 bytes × 7B ≈ 112 GB before activations. That
  calls for sharding, or PEFT for fine-tuning.
- **Why BF16 over FP16?** The same 8-bit exponent as FP32 gives the full range,
  so there is less overflow or underflow and no need for loss scaling. The
  cost is lower precision.
- **DDP vs. FSDP?** DDP replicates everything and adds speed only. FSDP shards
  parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, which adds capacity at a
  communication cost.
- **The three ZeRO stages?** Shard optimizer states; then also gradients; then
  also parameters.
- **What is $C \approx 6ND$?** The approximate training FLOPs for a dense
  transformer with $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens.
- **The Chinchilla result in one line?** For a fixed training-compute budget,
  scale parameters and tokens together, at about 20 tokens per parameter.
  Many earlier models were under-trained.
- **Why train beyond Chinchilla-optimal?** Serving costs dominate over a
  model's life. A smaller model trained on more data is cheaper to run at the
  same quality.
- **When would you pre-train a domain model?** When the domain language is
  distinctive, domain data is plentiful, the budget is large, and prompting,
  RAG, fine-tuning, and continued pre-training have been shown to fall short.
